content.overview: BNS s. 19 — Act likely to cause harm, but done without criminal intent, and to prevent other harm.
content.study:
Introduction and meaning
Act likely to cause harm, but done without criminal intent, and to prevent other harm. BNS restatement of IPC 81. Elements are substantially the same; cite the BNS number for offences on or after 1 July 2024. BNS restatement of IPC 81. Cite the BNS number for facts on or after 1 July 2024.
In student language: BNS s. 19 is the rule on “Act likely to cause harm, but done without criminal intent, and to prevent other harm”. The section provides that nothing is an offence merely by reason of its being done with the knowledge that it is likely to cause harm, if it be done without any criminal intention to cause harm, and in good faith for the purpose of preventing or avoiding other harm to person or property. Do not stop at the heading. An examiner awards marks for the ingredients, the explanations and the illustrations, not for writing the title alone.

Why this is asked
Criminal law arguments turn on statutory ingredients. BNS s. 19 exists so that “Act likely to cause harm, but done without criminal intent, and to prevent other harm” has a closed legal test in Chapter III — General Exceptions. An authoritative analysis defines the concept, lists every ingredient, walks the statutory illustrations, states exceptions, and applies the test methodically to facts.
Chapter setting: When an act is not an offence: mistake, accident, infancy, unsoundness, consent, compulsion — and the right of private defence.

The provision in detail
19. Nothing is an offence merely by reason of its being done with the knowledge that it is likely to cause harm, if it be done without any criminal intention to cause harm, and in good faith for the purpose of preventing or avoiding other harm to person or property

Essential ingredients
1. Nothing is an offence merely by reason of its being done with the knowledge that it is likely to cause harm, if it be done without any criminal intention to cause harm, and in good faith for the purpose of preventing or avoiding other harm to person or property

Statutory illustrations
Illustration (a). A, the captain of a vessel, suddenly and without any fault or negligence on his part, finds himself in such a position that, before he can stop his vessel, he must inevitably run down a boat B, with twenty or thirty passengers on board, unless he changes the course of his vessel, and that, by changing his course, he must incur risk of running down a boat C with only two passengers on board, which he may possibly clear. Here, if A alters his course without any intention to run down the boat C and in good faith for the purpose of avoiding the danger to the passengers in the boat B, he is not guilty of an offence, though he may run down the boat C by doing an act which he knew was likely to cause that effect, if it be found as a matter of fact that the danger which he intended to avoid was such as to excuse him in incurring the risk of running down the boat C

Exam use: quote illustration (a), then write which ingredient of BNS s. 19 it proves. Copying the illustration without that mapping sentence does not score.

Illustration (b). A, in a great fire, pulls down houses in order to prevent the conflagration from spreading. He does this with the intention in good faith of saving human life or property. Here, if it be found that the harm to be prevented was of such a nature and so imminent as to excuse A’s act, A is not guilty of the offence

Exam use: quote illustration (b), then write which ingredient of BNS s. 19 it proves. Copying the illustration without that mapping sentence does not score.

Explanations
Explanation.—It is a question of fact in such a case whether the harm to be prevented or avoided was of such a nature and so imminent as to justify or excuse the risk of doing the act with the knowledge that it was likely to cause harm

hypotheticals.question: Whether BNS s. 19 (Act likely to cause harm, but done without criminal intent, and to prevent other harm) applies, and how structured written arguments should be framed.
hypotheticals.analysis:
Step 1 — Identify the provision. The correct current-law cite is BNS s. 19 (Act likely to cause harm, but done without criminal intent, and to prevent other harm), Chapter III — General Exceptions.
Step 2 — State the legal test in your own words, then list the ingredients:
   (1) Nothing is an offence merely by reason of its being done with the knowledge that it is likely to cause harm, if it be done without any criminal intention to cause harm, and in good faith for the purpose of preventing or avoiding other harm to person or property
Step 3 — Read every Explanation. An explanation is part of the section. Omitting it leaves the analysis incomplete and vulnerable to rebuttal.
Step 4 — Map each fact to an ingredient. Write “this fact proves ingredient (a)” or “this fact is missing, so the section is not made out”.
Step 5 — Conclude. If every essential ingredient is proved and no exception covers the case, BNS s. 19 applies. If any essential ingredient fails, say so and stop. Do not invent a different section to save the answer.

learningObjectives: State the necessity rule in BNS s.19.
Apply the conditions of no criminal intention, good faith, and the purpose of preventing or avoiding other harm.
Explain that the choice between harms is a question of fact, using the vessel illustration.
enhancement.definition: BNS s.19 provides that nothing is an offence merely because it is done with knowledge that it is likely to cause harm, if it is done without any criminal intention to cause harm, and in good faith for the purpose of preventing or avoiding other harm to person or property.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: Knowledge that harm is likely does not by itself make the act an offence where the section's conditions are met. The act must be without criminal intention to cause harm, in good faith, and for the purpose of preventing or avoiding other harm to person or property.
statutoryFramework: Chapter III — General Exceptions, BNS s.19.
The act is done with knowledge that it is likely to cause harm.
It is done without any criminal intention to cause harm.
It is done in good faith for the purpose of preventing or avoiding other harm to person or property.

Illustration: the captain of a vessel, suddenly and without fault or negligence, must either run down boat B with twenty or thirty passengers or change course. If he changes course and runs down boat C in good faith to avoid the greater harm, he has committed no offence.

The explanation in the migrated text treats it as a question of fact whether the harm to be prevented or avoided was of such a nature and so imminent as to justify or excuse the risk of doing the act with that knowledge.
essentialIngredients: Knowledge that the act is likely to cause harm.
No criminal intention to cause harm.
The purpose is preventing or avoiding other harm to person or property.
The nature and imminence of the harm avoided, as against the risk taken, are questions of fact.
enhancement.detailedExplanation: Section 19 is the necessity exception, not the accident exception. The actor may know that harm is likely. The section says that knowledge alone does not make the act an offence if there is no criminal intention to cause harm and the act is done in good faith to prevent or avoid other harm to person or property. The vessel illustration is the working model: the captain, suddenly and without fault, must choose between running down a crowded boat and changing course onto a boat with fewer people. If the change is in good faith to avoid the greater harm, the illustration says there is no offence. The explanation makes the comparison a question of fact: whether the harm to be prevented was of such a nature and so imminent as to justify the risk. A student should not write that any chosen harm is excused. If the actor intends the harm, or does not act in good faith, the section does not apply.
examples: Statutory illustration, labelled as illustration: a captain, suddenly and without fault, changes course and runs down the smaller boat to avoid inevitably running down the crowded boat. If done in good faith to avoid the greater harm, no offence.
Teaching contrast: the captain changes course to strike an enemy's boat, intending that harm. The no-criminal-intention condition fails.
Teaching contrast: a hatchet head flies off during lawful work. That is the s.18 accident illustration, not a s.19 choice between harms.
distinctions: Section 18 is accident in a lawful act with proper caution. Section 19 is a known risk taken to avoid other harm.
Knowledge of likely harm is assumed in s.19. Criminal intention to cause harm is excluded.
The justification of the risk is a question of fact about nature and imminence, not a fixed formula.
problemApplication: Issue: whether knowledge of likely harm is excused by s.19.
Rule: no criminal intention; good faith; purpose of preventing or avoiding other harm to person or property; fact comparison of the harms.
Application: identify both harms, the imminence of the harm avoided, and the actor's intention.
Conclusion: excuse only if the statutory purpose and good faith are made out on the facts.

shortAnswer: State that knowledge of likely harm is not enough to convict if s.19 applies.
Add no criminal intention, good faith and the purpose of avoiding other harm.
Note that the comparison is a question of fact.
tenMark: Vessel illustration mapped to good faith and greater harm.
Explanation as a question of fact.
sixteenMark: Failure case where harm is intended.

keyTakeaways: Section 19 assumes knowledge and excludes criminal intention.
The purpose must be to prevent or avoid other harm to person or property.
Whether the risk was justified is a question of fact.
